paragraphs: Long ago, a full two thousand years ago now, there lived a rich man with a beautiful, devout wife, and they loved each other dearly. But they had no children, although they longed for them. The woman prayed day and night for a child, but still none came. In the courtyard in front of their house stood a juniper tree. One winter day, the woman stood beneath it peeling an apple. She cut her finger, and the blood fell onto the snow. “Ah,” she said with a deep sigh, looking sadly at the blood before her, “ah, if only I had a child as red as blood and as white as snow!” As she spoke, she suddenly felt happy, as though it were really going to happen. She went into the house. A month passed, and the snow was gone. Two months passed, and everything was green. Three months passed, and all the flowers sprang from the earth. Four months passed, and the trees in the wood grew thicker, their green branches closely intertwined. Birds sang until the wood echoed, and blossoms fell from the trees. Then the fifth month passed. She stood beneath the juniper tree, which smelled so sweet that her heart leapt. She fell to her knees, beside herself with joy. When the sixth month ended, the fruit was large and fine, and she grew very quiet. In the seventh month she snatched at the juniper berries and ate them greedily. Then she became sick and sad. The eighth month passed, and she called her husband to her. Weeping, she said, “If I die, bury me beneath the juniper tree.” After that she felt comforted and happy until the next month ended. Then she had a child as white as snow and as red as blood. When she saw it, she was so delighted that she died.
Her husband buried her beneath the juniper tree and wept bitterly. After a while he felt easier. He still wept, but he could bear it. After some more time, he married another woman.

His second wife had a daughter, while his first wife’s child was a little son, as red as blood and as white as snow. When the woman looked at her daughter, she loved her very much. But then she looked at the little boy, and it seemed to cut her to the heart. She thought he would always stand in her way. She was constantly thinking about how to get the whole fortune for her daughter. The Evil One filled her mind with this until she was furious with the little boy. She slapped him here and struck him there, until the unhappy child lived in constant terror. When he came home from school, he could find no peace anywhere.

One day the woman went upstairs to her room, and her little daughter followed. “Mother, give me an apple,” she said. “Yes, my child,” the woman replied, taking a fine apple from a chest. The chest had a great heavy lid and a large, sharp iron lock. “Mother,” the little girl asked, “isn’t my brother to have one too?” This angered the woman, but she said, “Yes, when he comes home from school.” When she looked out of the window and saw him coming, it was as though the Devil entered her. She snatched the apple back from her daughter. “You shall not have one before your brother,” she said. She threw the apple into the chest and closed it. Then the little boy came through the door, and the Devil made her say kindly, “My son, would you like an apple?” She looked wickedly at him. “Mother,” the boy said, “how dreadful you look! Yes, give me an apple.” Then she felt as though she were forced to say, “Come with me.” She lifted the chest’s lid. “Take an apple for yourself,” she said. As the little boy bent inside, the Devil prompted her, and crash! She slammed the lid shut. His head flew off and fell among the red apples. Terror overwhelmed her. “If only I could make them think I didn’t do it!” she thought. She went upstairs to her room, took a white handkerchief from the top drawer of her chest of drawers, and put the head back on the neck. She folded the handkerchief around it so that nothing showed, sat him on a chair in front of the door, and put the apple in his hand.

After this, Marlinchen went into the kitchen to her mother, who stood by the fire, constantly stirring a pan of hot water in front of her. “Mother,” Marlinchen said, “my brother is sitting at the door. He looks very white and has an apple in his hand. I asked him to give it to me, but he didn’t answer, and I was frightened.” “Go back,” her mother said. “If he won’t answer, slap him on the ear.” Marlinchen went to him. “Brother, give me the apple,” she said. He was silent, so she slapped his ear, and his head fell off. Terrified, Marlinchen began crying and screaming. She ran to her mother. “Oh, Mother, I’ve knocked my brother’s head off!” She wept and wept and could not be comforted. “Marlinchen,” her mother said, “what have you done? But be quiet and don’t let anyone know. It can’t be helped now. We’ll make him into blood sausages.” The mother took the little boy, chopped him into pieces, put him in the pan and made him into blood sausages. Marlinchen stood beside her, weeping and weeping. All her tears fell into the pan, so there was no need for salt.

Then the father came home and sat down to dinner. “But where is my son?” he asked. The mother served a great dish of blood sausages, while Marlinchen wept and could not stop. Again the father asked, “But where is my son?” “Oh,” the mother said, “he’s gone across the country to his mother’s great-uncle. He’ll stay there for a while.” “And what is he going to do there? He didn’t even say goodbye to me.”

“Oh, he wanted to go and asked whether he could stay six weeks. They’re taking good care of him.” “Ah,” the man said, “I feel so unhappy, afraid that something is wrong. He should have said goodbye to me.” He began to eat. “Marlinchen, why are you crying?” he asked. “Your brother will certainly come back.” Then he said, “Ah, wife, this food is delicious. Give me some more.” The more he ate, the more he wanted. “Give me more,” he said. “You shall have none. It seems as though it is all mine.” He ate and ate, throwing all the bones under the table, until he had finished everything. But Marlinchen went to her chest of drawers and took her best silk handkerchief from the bottom drawer. She gathered all the bones from under the table, tied them in her silk handkerchief, and carried them outside, weeping tears of blood. Then the juniper tree began to stir. Its branches parted and came together again as though someone were rejoicing and clapping their hands. At the same time, a mist seemed to rise from the tree. It burned like a fire at its centre, and a beautiful bird flew out of the fire, singing magnificently. He flew high into the air. Once he was gone, the juniper tree was just as it had been, and the handkerchief with the bones had vanished. Marlinchen, however, was as cheerful and happy as if her brother were still alive. She went merrily into the house, sat down to dinner and ate.
The bird flew away and landed on a goldsmith’s house. It began to sing:

“My mother killed me,
My father ate me,
My sister, little Marlinchen,
Gathered all my bones,
Tied them in a silk handkerchief,
Laid them beneath the juniper tree.
Kywitt, kywitt, what a beautiful bird I am!”

The goldsmith sat in his workshop making a gold chain. He heard the bird singing on his roof and thought the song very beautiful. He got up, but lost one of his slippers as he crossed the threshold. Still, he walked right up the middle of the street, with one shoe on and one sock. He wore his apron and carried the gold chain in one hand and his pincers in the other. The sun shone brightly on the street. He went on, stopped and spoke to the bird. “Bird,” he said, “how beautifully you sing! Sing that song again.” “No,” the bird said. “I won’t sing twice for nothing. Give me the gold chain, and I’ll sing it again for you.” “There,” the goldsmith said. “There is the gold chain. Now sing me that song again.” The bird came down, took the chain in his right claw, settled in front of the goldsmith, and sang:

“My mother killed me,
My father ate me,
My sister, little Marlinchen,
Gathered all my bones,
Tied them in a silk handkerchief,
Laid them beneath the juniper tree.
Kywitt, kywitt, what a beautiful bird I am!”
Then the bird flew to a shoemaker’s house, landed on the roof, and sang:

“My mother killed me,
My father ate me,
My sister, little Marlinchen,
Gathered all my bones,
Tied them in a silk handkerchief,
Laid them beneath the juniper tree.
Kywitt, kywitt, what a beautiful bird I am!”

The shoemaker heard him and ran outside in his shirtsleeves. He looked up at the roof, shielding his eyes with his hand so the sun would not blind him. “Bird,” he said, “how beautifully you sing!” Then he called through the doorway, “Wife, come outside. There’s a bird! Look at that bird—he certainly can sing!” He called his daughter and the other children, his apprentices, boys and girls. They all came up the street and looked at the bird. They saw how beautiful he was, with fine red and green feathers, a neck like real gold, and eyes shining like stars. “Bird,” the shoemaker said, “sing that song again.” “No,” the bird answered. “I don’t sing twice for nothing. You must give me something.” “Wife,” the man said, “go to the attic. There’s a pair of red shoes on the top shelf. Bring them down.” His wife went and fetched the shoes. “There, bird,” the man said. “Now sing that song again.” The bird came down, took the shoes in his left claw, flew back onto the roof, and sang:

“My mother killed me,
My father ate me,
My sister, little Marlinchen,
Gathered all my bones,
Tied them in a silk handkerchief,
Laid them beneath the juniper tree.
Kywitt, kywitt, what a beautiful bird I am!”

When he had finished the whole song, he flew away, carrying the chain in his right claw and the shoes in his left. He flew far away to a mill. The mill went “klipp klapp, klipp klapp, klipp klapp.” Inside sat twenty of the miller’s men, cutting and shaping a stone: hick hack, hick hack, hick hack. And the mill went klipp klapp, klipp klapp, klipp klapp. The bird settled in a lime tree in front of the mill and sang:
“My mother killed me,”
Then one man stopped working.
“My father ate me.”
Then two more stopped working and listened.
“My sister, little Marlinchen,”
Then four more stopped.

“Gathered all my bones,
Tied them in a silk handkerchief,”
Now only eight were cutting.
“Laid them beneath”
Now only five.
“The juniper tree,”
And now only one.
“Kywitt, kywitt, what a beautiful bird I am!”
Then the last man stopped too and heard the final words. “Bird,” he said, “how beautifully you sing! Let me hear it too. Sing it once more for me.”
“No,” the bird said. “I won’t sing twice for nothing. Give me the millstone, and I’ll sing it again.”
“Yes,” the man said. “If it belonged only to me, you could have it.”

“Yes,” the others said. “If he sings again, he shall have it.” The bird came down. All twenty millers set to work with a beam and lifted the stone. The bird put his neck through the hole and wore the stone like a collar. He flew back to the tree and sang:

“My mother killed me,
My father ate me,
My sister, little Marlinchen,
Gathered all my bones,
Tied them in a silk handkerchief,
Laid them beneath the juniper tree.
Kywitt, kywitt, what a beautiful bird I am!”
When he had finished, he spread his wings. With the chain in his right claw, the shoes in his left, and the millstone around his neck, he flew far away to his father’s house.

The father, mother and Marlinchen sat in the room eating dinner. “How light-hearted I feel!” the father said. “How happy I am!” “No,” the mother said, “I feel so uneasy, as though a great storm were coming.” Marlinchen sat weeping and weeping. Then the bird flew up and settled on the roof. “Ah,” the father said, “I feel truly happy. The sun is shining so beautifully outside. I feel as though I am about to see an old friend again.” “No,” the woman said, “I feel so anxious. My teeth are chattering, and there seems to be fire in my veins.” She tore open her corset. But Marlinchen sat crying in a corner, holding her plate in front of her eyes and weeping until it was quite wet. Then the bird settled in the juniper tree and sang:
“My mother killed me,”
The mother blocked her ears and closed her eyes, refusing to see or hear. But a roaring like the fiercest storm filled her ears, and her eyes burned and flashed like lightning.
“My father ate me,”
“Ah, Mother,” the man said, “what a beautiful bird! He sings so splendidly, the sun shines so warmly, and there’s a smell just like cinnamon.”
“My sister, little Marlinchen,”

Marlinchen laid her head on her knees and wept without stopping. But the man said, “I’m going out. I must see the bird close up.” “Oh, don’t go,” the woman said. “I feel as though the whole house is shaking and on fire.” But he went outside and looked at the bird:

“Gathered all my bones,
Tied them in a silk handkerchief,
Laid them beneath the juniper tree.
Kywitt, kywitt, what a beautiful bird I am!”

The bird dropped the gold chain. It fell exactly around the man’s neck, so perfectly that it fitted beautifully. He went inside and said, “Look what a fine bird that is! What a handsome gold chain he has given me, and how pretty he is!” But the woman was terrified. She fell to the floor, and her cap fell off her head. Then the bird sang again:
“My mother killed me.”
“If only I were a thousand feet beneath the earth, so I could not hear that!”
“My father ate me,”
Then the woman fell down again as though dead.
“My sister, little Marlinchen,”
“Ah,” Marlinchen said, “I’ll go out too, and see whether the bird will give me anything.” And she went outside.

“Gathered all my bones,
Tied them in a silk handkerchief,”
Then he threw the shoes down to her.

“Laid them beneath the juniper tree.
Kywitt, kywitt, what a beautiful bird I am!”

She became light-hearted and joyful, put on the new red shoes, and danced and leapt into the house. “Ah,” she said, “I was so sad when I went out, and now I feel so light-hearted! What a splendid bird—he has given me a pair of red shoes!” “Well,” the woman said, springing to her feet, her hair standing up like flames, “I feel as though the world is ending! I’ll go outside too and see whether my heart feels lighter.” As she stepped through the door, crash! The bird dropped the millstone onto her head and crushed her completely. The father and Marlinchen heard what had happened and went out. Smoke, flames and fire rose from the spot. When they cleared, the little brother stood there. He took his father and Marlinchen by the hand. All three were very happy, and they went inside to dinner and ate.
